process.name: Survey: name the systems
process.text: The survey counts workstations and names what stands on the floor — panel system manufacturer and line, connector type, built-ins, electronics per station, file runs — and walks both buildings' access. The destination floor plan is collected here; the move is built to it.

process.name: One flat rate in writing
process.text: The reviewed scope — stations, systems, buildings, windows — is priced at one flat rate in writing before work begins, built on the man-hour plan (station teardown and rebuild times are known quantities, not guesses).

process.name: Power and paperwork before panels
process.text: Building approvals and the COI run through the commercial packet; on the floor, circuits feeding panel runs are de-energized by the customer's or building's qualified person. No workstation is loosened on a live whip.

process.name: Label, then teardown in order
process.text: Every station is photographed and color-labeled to the destination plan. Teardown runs the fixed order: devices, mounted components, panels, rails, frame — hardware bagged with its station, panels stacked in labeled sequence, electronics wrapped and grouped by workstation.

process.name: Move in waves as scheduled
process.text: Freight moves in the building's windows — after-hours, weekend, or phased by department — with each wave a complete unit of labeled freight.

process.name: Rebuild to the plan
process.text: Stations stand back up in label order against the floor plan, connectors torqued and true, worksurfaces and overheads mounted, electronics placed by workstation for IT's reconnect pass.

process.name: Day-one walk-through
process.text: The office is walked desk by desk against the plan on the next business morning's side of the move: stations complete, file order intact, debris and protection gone, strays retrieved.

researchClaims.detail: The sequence is the skill: work surfaces, overheads, and mounted components come off first, panels lift out next — outermost first — connector rails and hardware are bagged and labeled with the station, and the frame comes down last. Run the sequence backwards, or lose the hardware bag, and reassembly day becomes a parts hunt.
researchClaims.fact: A cubicle system is engineered modularity: panels, connector rails, and frames designed to come apart and reconfigure. Disassembly runs in a fixed order — disconnect power and devices, remove built-in cabinets, desks, and shelves mounted to the panels, remove panels, detach connector rails, then break down the frame. Everything mounted to a panel must come off before the panel can move.
researchClaims.headline: Cubicle teardown runs in one order — reverse it and parts break
researchClaims.scope: Systems-furniture construction and disassembly practice as installers document it; applies to the major panel systems (Steelcase, Herman Miller, Haworth, Knoll class).

source.title: How to Disassemble an Office Cubicle for Moving

researchClaims.detail: Data and voice cables run their own paths through the same panels and are uncoupled and traced separately, so destination reconnect starts from labeled ends, not a tangle. An office move that loosens a panel on a live whip risks the crew, the equipment, and the building's panel schedule — the power check is step zero, not a detail.
researchClaims.fact: Panel systems carry their power with them: pre-wired electrical whips run through the base or spine of the panels, feeding outlets and lighting at each station. Before any panel is loosened, the circuit feeding the run must be de-energized at the junction box or breaker panel. Moving a panel against a live whip is an electric-shock and equipment-damage hazard.
researchClaims.headline: The power whip comes first: panels move only on a dead circuit
researchClaims.scope: Electrical safety practice for systems furniture as installer guidance states it; de-energizing is performed by the customer's or building's qualified person (see boundary OFF-B1).

source.title: How to Disassemble Cubicles for Moving or Storage

researchClaims.detail: That two-person, sub-hour figure is the planning unit of an office move: station count multiplied by teardown and rebuild time, plus transit and building windows, is the schedule — and it is why office estimates are built on man-hours (the commercial research layer, L2-COM-04) rather than on the weight of the furniture.
researchClaims.fact: Timed on real workstations: a standard two-panel cubicle takes two people 30 to 45 minutes to disassemble once tools are staged and cables are disconnected. Larger stations with built-in cabinets, shelving, or non-standard connector hardware take an hour or more each.
researchClaims.headline: A two-panel workstation is 30 to 45 minutes of teardown, timed
researchClaims.scope: Trade timing for a standard station with power and devices already disconnected; quoted as the installer community's typical figure, not a per-job promise.

source.title: How to Disassemble an Office Cubicle for Moving — disassembly timing

researchClaims.detail: A crew that has only ever fought one brand's connectors will learn the second brand's at the customer's expense, on the customer's clock. The survey names the system on the floor — manufacturer, product line, connector type — so teardown day starts with the right tools already staged.
researchClaims.fact: Connector hardware is manufacturer-specific. Steelcase's Answer, Kick, and Montage panels typically release on spring-loaded connector clips pressed and lifted at the panel edge — no unscrewing. Other systems use connector rods, bolts, gravity locks, or interlocking spline connections, each with its own release method and tools.
researchClaims.headline: Every panel brand connects differently — the survey names the system
researchClaims.scope: Manufacturer systems as installer guides document them; the named Steelcase lines are the guide's own examples.

source.title: How to Disassemble an Office Cubicle for Moving — tips by cubicle brand

researchClaims.detail: Color-coding does double duty: at origin it groups a station's parts for the truck, and at destination it routes them — a color per department or zone, a number per station, matched to the floor plan the customer supplies. The plan and the labels are one system; either one alone is half a system.
researchClaims.fact: Workstation moves run on a labeling discipline: color-coded labels tie every panel, connector, worksurface, and hardware bag to its destination position on the new floor plan, and removed panels are stacked in labeled sequence so the rebuild happens in order rather than by search.
researchClaims.headline: Color-coded labels are the move's memory
researchClaims.scope: Industry labeling practice across commercial movers' published methods; destination plans are the customer's document (boundary OFF-B3).

source.title: Office Movers — Cubicle Disassembly and Reassembly

researchClaims.detail: Phasing follows the same discipline per wave: each department's freight is labeled, moved, and rebuilt as a unit against the plan, so Monday's returning staff find their department standing — while the next wave is still being packed at origin.
researchClaims.fact: Office moves are scheduled around the business, not the truck: after-hours and weekend windows, and for larger floors a phased sequence — department by department — so the organization keeps working while it moves. The finish line is not an unloaded truck; it is employees at working desks on the next business day.
researchClaims.headline: The finish line is Monday morning: desks working, not trucks empty
researchClaims.scope: Scheduling practice as the commercial moving trade documents it (IOMI downtime doctrine applied at office scale).

source.title: Office Moving & Commercial Relocation — downtime, phasing, after-hours scheduling

researchClaims.detail: The same thinking governs the file room and the supply shelves: anything whose order is its value travels in its order. Boxing is reserved for what genuinely packs; rolling systems carry the working collections, and the map of which cart serves which destination zone rides with the labels.
researchClaims.fact: For libraries, file runs, and shelved records, the office-moving method loads rolling book carts — effectively bookcases on wheels — under supervision, keeping volumes in shelf order and accessible immediately before and after the move, instead of packing them into boxes where order is lost and the collection is out of service on both ends of the trip.
researchClaims.headline: Files travel in order: rolling carts, not mountains of boxes
researchClaims.scope: IOMI's published method for library and file moves, quoted as domain practice.

source.title: 10 Steps to a Successful Office Move (IOMI methods — book bins)

@graph.name: Office Moving — Scope Boundaries
@graph.description: The scope boundaries of the office moving category stated as data. Electrical feeds are cut and restored by the customer's or building's qualified person — the crew disassembles furniture around a dead circuit and performs no electrical work. Reconnection ends with the right equipment on the right desk in the right order; network configuration and systems administration stay with the customer's IT. Reassembly builds to the destination floor plan the customer supplies; redesigns are the customer's and their space planner's decisions, and conflicts found on the floor are flagged in the open before anyone builds around them.

boundaries.name: Power is cut by the building's side, panels come apart on the mover's side
boundaries.text: Cubicle power whips are de-energized at the panel or junction box by the customer's or the building's qualified person before any workstation is loosened, and the feed is reconnected the same way at destination. The moving crew disassembles and reassembles the furniture system around a dead circuit — it does not wire, splice, or certify electrical work.

boundaries.name: Reconnection is IT's finish line
boundaries.text: Workstations are placed, grouped, and sequenced so the customer's IT team can reconnect in order — but network configuration, imaging, and systems administration stay with IT. The mover's job ends with the right equipment on the right desk in the right order; the login screen is IT's.

boundaries.name: The floor plan is the customer's document
boundaries.text: Reassembly follows the destination floor plan the customer supplies. Mid-move redesigns — different cluster shapes, moved power feeds — are construction and design decisions that belong to the customer and their space planner; the crew builds to the plan it was given and flags conflicts it finds, in the open, before building around them.
